title: Google Voice personal vs business: 8 key differences
summary: What’s the difference between Google Voice personal vs business plans? This guide explains all eight major differences.
body_markdown:
Trying to understand the differences between Google Voice’s personal and business plans?


Here’s a quick overview of the differences:


- **Number of users.** Personal Voice plans only allow one user on the account, while Google for Business plans can accommodate multiple users.
- **Availability.** Personal Voice plans are only for US customers, while Google for Business supports users from 14 countries.
- **Phone numbers.** Google allows personal Voice users to have one additional phone number ported from an existing mobile number, while Google Voice for business accounts can have one number per user.
- **Integrations.** Only Google Voice for business users can integrate with other Google apps.


We’ll go over these points in more detail, as well as review pricing plans. And if you don’t like[how Google Voice works](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-does-google-voice-work/) , we’ll offer a modern business phone alternative.


##


**Google Voice personal vs business compared at a glance**


Google Voice plans fall into two categories: personal and business. Each tier has its own set of features and requirements. We’ll cover each category separately. First, the personal plans:


### **A quick look at the Google Voice personal plans**


The Google Voice personal plans have three tiers, including a free tier with basic features:

Monthly pricing per user Free $10 $20


Pricing note Requires personal Gmail account Requires personal Gmail account Requires personal Gmail account

AI note-taking X X ✔


Call recording Inbound only, on-demand On-demand On-demand


All personal plans are only available in the US. You can use unlimited calling and messaging in the US and Canada, but none of the personal plans integrate with other Google apps. To do that, you’ll need to upgrade to Google Voice for business. However, even after you upgrade, you can’t integrate Google Voice with any third-party apps.


Each of the personal plans i breaks down like this:


- **Personal:** One free user with two numbers for unlimited calling and messaging to the US and Canada
- **Starter with Voice:** $10 for one user per month for on-demand call recording and desk phone support
- **Voice Standard:** $20 for one user per month for AI note-taking and auto-attendants


### **A quick look at the Google Voice for business plans**


If you’re considering using Google Voice as part of a team, here’s what the Google Voice for business plans look like side by side:


Voice Starter for business Voice Standard for business Voice Premier for business

All Google Voice for business subscriptions have everything the personal plans do, like three-way calling, unlimited calling, and unlimited messaging, but they’re available in 14 countries, not just the US. These plans also include AI note-taking and integrations with Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Meet. These plans require a Google Workspace subscription, which starts at $7 per user per month, so total pricing is actually higher.


Here’s how the Google Voice for business plans are priced:


- **Voice Starter:** $10 per user per month with a maximum of 10 seats
- **Voice Standard:** $20 per user per month for unlimited seats, multi-level auto-attendant, ring groups, call delegation, and custom hold audio
- **Voice Premier: $** 30 per user per month for unlimited seats, advanced reporting, automatic call recording, and the ability to get additional numbers outside your home country


##


**A deeper look at the key differences between Google Voice personal vs business**


Google Voice’s personal and business plans share a few similarities. Both offer a VoIP service that lets you make or take calls through a WiFi connection. They also let you make unlimited calls from your internet browser or mobile device.


But that’s where the similarities end. Google Voice personal is a personal communications app for private individuals or solopreneurs. Google Voice for business is designed to be a business phone system for teams.


Here are the eight key differences between Google Voice personal vs business plans:


### **1. Pricing and fees for Google Voice personal vs business**


Let’s get it out of the way: yes, Google Voice has a free plan. Yes, it gives you unlimited calling and messaging within the US and Canada. But it also offers paid plans in the personal category that expand capabilities for solo operators who need them.


Since they’re intended for solo users, Google Voice’s personal plans are limited in the features they offer — the free account especially.


The free account lets you record calls, but only on demand for inbound calls. And while it allows two numbers, you can only use one at a time. The second number has to be ported in from a mobile carrier.


Paid single-user accounts include a few more features, like three-way calling and auto-attendants, but they’re still more limited than the Google Voice for business plans.


Google Voice for business plans allow for more team members — 10 for the lowest business plan and unlimited for both higher tiers. They’re available in more regions and have more business-friendly features.


Just know that each Google Voice for business plan requires an active Google Workspace subscription, which costs $7 a month. This is in addition to what you pay for Google Voice.


Given these conditions, many people look for an[alternative to Google Voice](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-alternatives/) .


### **2. Availability of each Google Voice plan**


Google Voice’s personal plans are only available in the US. You can make[international calls with Google Voice](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-international-calls/) while abroad, but you can’t purchase a number from outside the US.


Google Voice for business is available outside the US. However, it’s limited to specific countries:


- Belgium
- Canada
- Denmark
- France
- Germany
- Ireland
- Italy
- Netherlands
- Portugal
- Spain
- Sweden (Stockholm, Malmö, and Göteborg)
- Switzerland
- The UK
- The continental US


If you live in Alaska, Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, or the US Virgin Islands, you can’t access Google Voice.


Some international locations can use Google Voice’s SIP Link to make calls through their existing cell phone carriers. If you make a call through your Google Voice number, you either use minutes from your cell phone plan or pay international calling fees, depending on your subscription. This applies to businesses in:


- Argentina
- Brazil
- Chile
- Colombia
- Mexico


Keep in mind you need to upgrade to the business Standard plan to unlock Google Voice’s SIP Link capabilities. Then you pay extra fees — which aren’t listed online — for either SIP Link Standard or SIP Link Premier. Google Voice also says that your SIP link international call rates may differ from what’s on their website. This means you may pay more to reach customers overseas.


### **3. Only one user is allowed on the personal plans**


Google Voice won’t let you have multiple users on any personal accounts. So you won’t be able to add team members to your system and connect them.


You’ll need Google Voice for business if you want to add multiple users to an account.


### **4. Texting is limited to US customers**


Google Voice’s personal plans let you send and receive SMS and MMS messages. But since they weren’t built for business use, you can’t send mass texts or add more than seven people to a group chat. Sending[MMS messages with Google Voice](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-mms/) has several caveats, including the option to only send photos as attachments or links. You may also hit[Google Voice’s text limits](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-texting-limit/) and get blocked. In some cases, you may not receive any indication of when or if you’ll be able to text with your number again.


And text messaging is only available to US customers.


Google Voice for Google Workspace offers unlimited texting to anyone you contact in the US. But like the free plan, you must be based in the US to send messages when using a[Google business phone number](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-for-business/#how-to-get-a-google-phone-number-for-business-in-5-steps) . Even if you are a customer in the US, you still won’t have options to save time while texting. You can’t[schedule text messages](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-schedule-texts/) unless you use the scheduling function in Gmail, and[templated snippets](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/messaging/snippets) aren’t available on any Voice plan. Google Voice doesn’t support automating specific touchpoints through text.


If not having SMS is a problem for your small business, you may want to consider a Google Voice alternative or a[business texting app](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-business-texting-services/) .


### **5. Ring groups are exclusive to Google Voice for business**


Google Voice’s free plan doesn’t offer ring groups. Remember: it wasn’t designed for anything more than personal phone calls.


With Google Voice for business, you can use ring groups to ring different devices and ensure someone is always around to answer the phone. This helps your team members split responsibility for incoming calls by ringing specific groups at the same time.


There are several reasons to use ring groups for your business. For example, you could set up a[ring group](https://www.quo.com/features/ring-groups) that calls all members of your customer support team at the same time. Customers have someone around to answer their questions, while your coworkers can handle incoming calls more effectively as a team.


But Google Voice’s ring groups aren’t a perfect solution for call collaboration. You still can’t collaborate in-app as a team or respond to incoming texts as a group — unlike other[VoIP solutions](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-voip-service/) . Ring groups also require the Voice Standard plan, which is $20 per user per month, plus the $7 Google Workspace subscription.


### **6. Porting costs extra on Google Voice’s personal plans**


Both Google Voice’s free version and Google Voice for business let you[port over existing numbers](https://www.quo.com/blog/whats-phone-number-porting/) . This is free for Google Voice for business users, but not for personal plan users.


[Porting a number into Google Voice’s](https://www.quo.com/blog/port-number-to-google-voice/) personal plan costs $20. If you decide to port out, you have to pay an additional $3 unlocking fee. Otherwise, your number stays in Google Voice indefinitely.


### **7. Google Voice offers limited integration options**


The free plan of Google Voice doesn’t let you connect with integrations.


Google Voice for business only integrates with other Google apps, including Google Meet and Google Calendar. No other apps are supported at this time, and none are planned for the future.


The best VoIP service providers help businesses connect with the tools in their tech stack. For example, platforms like Quo can help you[push updated contact information](https://www.quo.com/blog/openphone-hubspot-integration/) to your company CRM. They can also help you build workflows that sync texts and voicemails across multiple channels, including email and Slack.


### **8. Business contact management is more challenging on personal plans**


Google Voice for business operates separately from your phone plan, which makes it easier to keep some distance between[your personal number](https://www.quo.com/blog/using-personal-phone-for-work/) and your professional career.


However, Google Voice’s free plan stores your business contacts in the Google Contacts app — which means they’re synced alongside your personal contacts. You won’t get notifications that distinguish work calls from personal calls, which could make it hard to know when to answer.


##


**What are you missing out on with both Google Voice personal and business plans?**


Although Google Voice’s business plans offer more than the free personal version, both are missing several critical features that small business owners need.


Here are all the[cons for Google Voice](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-pros-and-cons/#cons) :


- **No clear conversations.** All your calls, texts, and voice messages live in separate folders within Google Voice. This means it can take longer to review conversations and makes it harder to follow up with past context.
- **No auto-replies.** You can’t automatically send text messages if you miss a call or voice message. This means you have to stay connected to your phone all day if you want to set client expectations.
- **No options to save time texting.** You can’t text customers at all if you’re outside the US, which is a dealbreaker for international companies. But even if you are in the US, you won’t be able to queue texts to send later, save go-to texts as templates, or access other features that could save time for your team.
- **No toll-free numbers.**[Google Voice doesn’t support toll-free numbers](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-toll-free-numbers/) , so you can’t help your small business look more professional to customers as it grows. And if you already have a toll-free number, you can’t port it into Google Voice.
- **No desktop app.** Google Voice doesn’t have a dedicated desktop app, so you can’t access your phone service from your computer. You have to log in through a browser or rely on your cell phone to make or take calls. If you or your team prefer a dedicated app to receive calls on your computer, Google Voice won’t work for you.
- **No internal messaging.** You can’t[collaborate with your teammates](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/team-collaboration/internal-threads#adding-thread-comments) on responses to customers inside Google Voice. Instead, you have to rely on another Google app like Hangouts or Chat, which forces you to switch between apps.
- **Limited text forwarding.** Both versions of Google Voice prevent you from forwarding texts to other tools, including platforms like Slack. You can only forward texts to Gmail, which isn’t helpful if you don’t have a company Gmail account.
- **No automations.** With Google Voice, you can’t[automate specific touchpoints](https://www.quo.com/product/messaging/automated-text-messages) with your customers. You also can’t automate repetitive tasks, which reduces the time you can focus on more compelling work.
- **No true team collaboration.** Google Voice lacks team collaboration features that most other business phone solutions provide, like shared inboxes and internal threads. This makes it harder for your team to get a complete picture of a caller’s history.
- **No AI receptionist.** Many modern business phone solutions, like Quo, offer AI receptionists that can help you answer calls 24/7, capture leads, and redirect calls to other team members. Google Voice has an auto-attendant, but that’s far less capable than an AI receptionist.
- **No third-party integrations.** Most business phone platforms integrate with other tools in the company’s tech stack, whether natively or through services like Zapier and Make. Google Voice doesn’t.


##


**Which Google Voice plan is right for you?**


It can be difficult to compare the pros and cons of six different plans, even with charts, so we’re going to make recommendations based on your business size and needs:


- **Google Voice personal.** Best suited for individuals like freelancers with clients in the US who only need basic calling.
- **Google Voice Starter.** A fit for solo business owners or consultants who need better calling features, specifically for recording and transcribing calls and voicemails.
- **Google Voice Standard.** Good for solo businesses that get enough inbound calls to require an auto-attendant and AI-assisted call documentation.
- **Google Voice for business Starter.** Meant for small business owners who already use other Google apps, with up to 10 employees who need phones and basic calling features.
- **Google Voice for business Standard.** Best for small and mid-sized businesses that need calls routed across different departments or handled by multiple employees.
- **Google Voice for business Premier.** Most suited to large enterprises and multinational businesses that need call record-keeping and advanced reporting.

##


**FAQs**


**What’s the difference between Google Voice personal plans and Google Voice for businesses?**


The personal plans only allow one user and are only available in the US. The Google Voice for business plans have more business-friendly features and allow multiple users per plan.


**Does Google Voice have a free plan?**


Google Voice has a free personal plan that lets you make unlimited calls and texts in the US, but it’s limited to one user and only records inbound calls on demand. The other two personal plans, Starter and Standard, are paid.


**Do I need a Google Workspace subscription?**


You don’t need a Google Workspace subscription for the three Google Voice personal plans, but you do need one for the business plans.


**Does Google Voice integrate with other Google products?**


Google Voice for business integrates with Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Meet.


**Does Google Voice integrate with any other apps?**


No, Google Voice only integrates with Google products.


**Can I make unlimited calls and texts with Google Voice?**


You can make unlimited calls in the US and Canada if your billing country is either of those two countries. However, text messages are available only to US customers.


**Can I use a personal Google Voice number for my business?**


You can port a personal mobile number into your personal Google Voice plan. There will be a one-time fee of $20.


**What are the pros and cons of Google Voice for personal use?**


Here are the biggest[Google Voice pros and cons](https://www.quo.com/blog/google-voice-pros-and-cons/) :


Pros
– The account is free
– Calling is free within the US and Canada
– Messaging is free within the US


Cons
– You can only record incoming calls
– You can’t share numbers with your team
– You can’t schedule texts or automate texting workflows
– You can’t integrate with Gmail or any other Google apps
– You don’t have access to business-friendly features like AI note-taking or call transfers


**Can I upgrade from a personal Google Voice plan to Workspace?**


You can upgrade a personal Google Voice plan to a Google Voice for business plan, provided you also sign up for a Google Workspace account for $7 a month.
